1.title: Authentication Mechanisms
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: Authentication Mechanisms. This module covers the task statement: apply authentication mechanisms. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Update V P C (Virtual Private Cloud) security groups so only the right sources reach data stores. Create and update I A M (Identity and Access Management) groups, roles, endpoints and services. Create and rotate credentials with A W S Secrets Manager. Set up I A M roles for Lambda, A P I Gateway, the A W S C L I (command line interface) and CloudFormation. Apply I A M policies to roles, endpoints and services (S three Access Points, A W S PrivateLink). Describe managed versus unmanaged services.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Locks the Doors
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Locks the Doors. The Redshift cluster is reachable from the whole internet. A Glue job cannot connect to the billing database. An analyst keeps a database password in a script. Your job: authenticate every caller and open only the paths that are needed.

1.title: Network Access: VPC Security Groups
1.text: Network Access: V P C Security Groups. The figure shows this: Security groups: a stateful firewall on the resource; allow rules only; reference another security group as the source; return traffic is automatic. A security group is a virtual firewall at the resource level (network interface): allow rules only, stateful (return traffic is allowed automatically), default deny for inbound.

1.title: Network Access: VPC Security Groups, continued
1.text: Network Access: V P C Security Groups, continued. Update rules to least access: allow only the needed port and source: Redshift five four three nine, PostgreSQL five four three two, MySQL three three zero six, H T T P S four hundred forty-three; use another security group as the source (for example the Glue job's) instead of an I P range; never open zero point zero.zero point zero or zero to a data store. Glue, E M R (Elastic MapReduce) and Lambda in a V P C: Glue connections use security groups with a self-referencing inbound rule (the group allows traffic from itself) so the job's workers can talk to each other. Network A C L s (access control list) are stateless subnet-level filters (allow and deny rules) and are not the main control for data stores.

1.title: Network Access: VPC Security Groups, continued
1.text: Network Access: V P C Security Groups, continued. Private connectivity: V P C endpoints (below) keep traffic off the internet; place data stores in private subnets. Exam tip: "Allow a Glue job to reach a private database" to a database security group rule that allows the job's security group (and the right port), not a public I P range.

1.title: IAM Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services
1.text: I A M Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services. The figure shows this: Who is calling: people use I A M Identity Center or I A M users in groups; services and workloads assume I A M roles with a trust policy and temporary credentials.

1.title: IAM Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued
1.text: I A M Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued. I A M user. Use: A person or app with long-term credentials. Remember: Avoid for workloads; use M F A (multi-factor authentication). I A M group. Use: Collection of users sharing permissions. Remember: Attach policies to the group, not each user. I A M role. Use: An identity with no long-term credentials that a trusted entity assumes to get temporary credentials. Remember: Preferred for services, applications and cross-account access. Trust policy. Use: Who may assume the role. Remember: Separate from the permissions policy (what the role may do). Service-linked role. Use: A role predefined for an A W S service. Remember: Created and managed by the service.

1.title: IAM Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued
1.text: I A M Identities: Groups, Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued. Federation (I A M Identity Center). Use: People sign in with corporate identities and get temporary role access. Remember: Best for human access to many accounts.

1.title: IAM roles for services and tools
1.text: I A M roles for services and tools. A W S Lambda. An execution role (trust: lambda.amazonaws.com) with permissions to the data stores and CloudWatch Logs. A W S Glue jobs and crawlers. A Glue service role that can read the sources, write the targets, use the Data Catalog and the temp bucket. Amazon A P I Gateway. I A M authorization for callers; an integration role so the A P I can call Lambda, Step Functions or other services. A W S C L I and S D K s (software development kit). Assume a role (named profile, I A M Identity Center sign-in, or environment) to get temporary credentials; never embed long-term keys.

1.title: IAM roles for services and tools, continued
1.text: I A M roles for services and tools, continued. A W S CloudFormation. A service role that CloudFormation assumes to create resources, so deployers need fewer direct permissions. Amazon E C two (Elastic Compute Cloud) or E C S (Elastic Container Service) or E K S (Elastic Kubernetes Service). Instance profile or task or pod role. Redshift, E M R, Step Functions, SageMaker. Roles attached to the cluster or state machine (for example the Redshift I A M role used by copy, unload and Spectrum). Cross-account access: the data owner's role trusts the other account; the caller assumes the role (S T S (Security Token Service) AssumeRole).

1.title: Endpoints
1.text: Endpoints. A V P C endpoint lets resources in your V P C reach A W S services privately: gateway endpoints (S three and DynamoDB; a route table entry; no extra charge) and interface endpoints (A W S PrivateLink: an elastic network interface with a private I P for many services, including your own). Update endpoints to add services, route tables, subnets and security groups, and endpoint policies. Exam tip: "A Lambda function needs to read S three and write Kinesis without long-term keys" to an I A M execution role with those permissions. "Keep S three traffic off the internet" to a gateway V P C endpoint.

1.title: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials
1.text: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials. The figure shows this: A W S Secrets Manager: applications fetch credentials at run time with an I A M role; rotation changes the password in both the secret and the database on a schedule. A W S Secrets Manager stores, retrieves and rotates database credentials, A P I keys and tokens; secrets are encrypted with A W S K M S (Key Management Service); access is controlled by I A M. Applications fetch the secret at run time, so no password lives in code, job parameters or configuration files.

1.title: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials, continued
1.text: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials, continued. Rotation: automatic rotation on a schedule (rate() or cron()); managed rotation (no Lambda to write) for Amazon R D S (Relational Database Service) and Aurora master user credentials and the Redshift admin password; other secrets use a Lambda rotation function (created from a template or your own) that must reach both Secrets Manager and the database over the network. Rotation steps (create new secret version, set it in the database, test, finish) keep the old version available until the switch, so applications do not break.

1.title: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials, continued
1.text: Secrets: Creating and Rotating Credentials, continued. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store also holds configuration and secrets (SecureString, encrypted with K M S) but has no built-in rotation (Module fifteen). Glue connections and Redshift can reference a secret instead of a password. Exam tip: "Rotate the R D S password automatically and have applications keep working" to Secrets Manager rotation (managed for R D S and Aurora).

2.title: Applying IAM Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services
2.text: Applying I A M Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services. Identity-based policy: attached to a user, group or role; says what it may do. Resource-based policy: attached to a resource (S three bucket, K M S key, S Q S (Simple Queue Service) queue, Lambda function, secret); names a principal (including other accounts). V P C endpoint policy: a resource policy on the endpoint that limits which principals and actions can use it (for example only your bucket).

2.title: Applying IAM Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued
2.text: Applying I A M Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued. Amazon S three Access Points: named network endpoints for a bucket, each with its own access point policy (and optionally restricted to one V P C): they simplify permissions for shared datasets (give each team or application its own access point instead of one huge bucket policy). A W S PrivateLink: private connectivity to a service (A W S, a partner or your own) over interface endpoints, no internet gateway, N A T (network address translation) or public I P; combine with endpoint policies. Evaluation: an explicit deny wins; otherwise something must allow; same-account access needs an allow in either the identity or the resource policy, cross-account needs both (Module fifteen).

2.title: Applying IAM Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued
2.text: Applying I A M Policies to Roles, Endpoints and Services, continued. Condition keys such as the source V P C endpoint condition (the endpoint) and the principal organization I D condition restrict access to a V P C endpoint or your organization. Exam tip: "Allow only requests from the company's V P C endpoint to read a bucket" to a bucket policy (or access point policy) with an the source V P C endpoint condition condition, plus the endpoint.

2.title: Managed versus Unmanaged Services
2.text: Managed versus Unmanaged Services. Examples. Managed services: R D S, Aurora, Redshift, DynamoDB, Glue, Athena, E M R Serverless, M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka), OpenSearch Service. Unmanaged (self-managed) services: A database installed on E C two, a self-built Kafka or Hadoop cluster. A W S manages. Managed services: Hardware, host and often the engine software, patching, backups, high availability, scaling options. Unmanaged (self-managed) services: Only the underlying infrastructure. You manage. Managed services: Data, access control, network settings, configuration, encryption choices. Unmanaged (self-managed) services: The operating system, patches, engine upgrades, backups, high availability, security hardening. Trade-off. Managed services: Less operational work; less control. Unmanaged (self-managed) services: Full control; much more work and risk.

2.title: Managed versus Unmanaged Services, continued
2.text: Managed versus Unmanaged Services, continued. This is the shared responsibility model: A W S secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it; the more managed the service, the more A W S handles. Prefer managed (or serverless) services for least operational overhead and built-in security features such as automatic patching, backups and encryption. Exam tip: "Least operational overhead" almost always points to a managed or serverless service.

2.title: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects
2.text: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects. The figure shows this: SageMaker Unified Studio structure: a domain at the top, domain units for business units or teams, and projects as the collaboration boundary where members work with data and tools. Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is a single workspace for data, analytics and A I (artificial intelligence) (notebooks, S Q L, visual E T L (extract, transform, load), catalog, and generative A I help). This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

2.title: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects, continued
2.text: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects, continued. Domain: the top-level container for an organization's users, groups, projects, catalog and settings; an administrator creates it and manages who can sign in (for example through I A M Identity Center). Domain units: hierarchy under a domain to model business units or teams; owners set policies for the projects in their unit; if none exist, everything sits at the root domain. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

2.title: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects, continued
2.text: SageMaker Unified Studio: Domains, Domain Units and Projects, continued. Projects: the collaboration boundary where members work on a business use case with shared data, compute and tools; members have roles (owner, contributor) and access depends on authorization policies. Why it matters for security: who may create projects, who is a member, and which data a project may see are controlled at these levels, and the business catalog (Module seven) and data sharing (Module eighteen) follow the same structure. Exam tip: "Separate teams or business units with their own policies and projects inside one governed workspace" to SageMaker Unified Studio domain units and projects. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Security groups: Stateful, allow-only, default deny inbound; allow specific port and source security group. I A M identities: Roles (temporary credentials, trust plus permissions policy) for services; groups for users; I A M Identity Center for people. Role setups: Lambda execution role, Glue service role, A P I Gateway integration role and I A M auth, C L I assume role or S S O (single sign-on), CloudFormation service role, Redshift or E M R or Step Functions roles. Endpoints: Gateway (S three, DynamoDB; route table; free) versus interface or PrivateLink (E N I, private I P); endpoint policies. Secrets Manager: Stores or rotates credentials, K M S encrypted; managed rotation for R D S or Aurora master and Redshift admin. Policies: Identity versus resource versus endpoint policy; S three Access Points (own policy, optional V P C-only); PrivateLink.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A Glue job runs in a V P C and must connect to a private Amazon Redshift cluster. What is the most secure network setting? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Referencing the job's security group as the source opens only the needed port to only that resource.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The database password for an Amazon R D S instance must be rotated automatically without breaking applications, and the team does not want to write code. What should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Secrets Manager rotates R D S and Aurora master credentials on a schedule with managed rotation, and applications fetch the current secret at run time.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which description of managed versus unmanaged services is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Managed services shift infrastructure and software maintenance to A W S; the customer is still responsible for data, access and configuration.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Several teams share one SageMaker Unified Studio domain. The company wants each business unit to set its own policies for who can create projects. Which feature provides this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Domain units model business-unit hierarchies, and their owners set policies for the projects in their unit.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all four answers. Question one: B. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
